title: Quantization performance deep dive (FP8 vs INT8) - Summit AI
topics: Current serving stack + pain points (latency variance, cost, long prompts)
Workload breakdown: prefill-heavy vs decode-heavy; batch/concurrency patterns
FP8 vs INT8 trade-offs on H100/A100; when wins show up
Pilot benchmark plan and success criteria
next_steps: Redwood to share pilot benchmark plan + runbook (workload definitions, env pinning, metrics) and a minimal script bundle to run in Summit’s VPC.
Summit to provide 3 representative prompt distributions (short chat, long-context RAG, summarization) and target gen-lengths + concurrency envelope.
Schedule a 30-min follow-up to review pilot results and decide: Hosted vs Dedicated H100 pool, and whether FP8 default is acceptable for their long-context workload.
If quality deltas show up under INT8/FP8, run Redwood sanity eval pack on Summit’s prompts and decide gating rules (by route/model/seq-len).
action_items: Henry Cho - Send Redwood benchmarking methodology + what we can/can’t claim externally (footnotes, variance) - due 2026-02-24
Grace Kim - Provide recommended benchmark matrix (H100 + A100 optional, FP16 baseline vs FP8 vs INT8, 3 seq-len regimes) - due 2026-02-24
Omar El-Sayed - Share notes on scheduler knobs to keep TTFT stable under higher batching (prefill/decode split instrumentation) - due 2026-02-25
Ava Chen - Confirm which environment Summit wants for pilot (their VPC vs Redwood Dedicated trial) and share security constraints for trace/artifact uploads - due 2026-02-25
Miguel Santos - Deliver 200–500 anonymized prompts or synthetic equivalents + acceptance thresholds (p50/p95 TTFT/TPOT) - due 2026-02-26
summary: Summit AI walked through three primary production workloads (short chat, long-context RAG, and summarization) and asked for defensible numbers on H100 for FP8 vs INT8, with a focus on p95 latency and cost predictability. Redwood explained that FP8 tends to produce the most consistent throughput wins on H100 in prefill-heavy regimes and at higher concurrency, while INT8 can be shape- and calibration-dependent and may require stricter guardrails (and sometimes doesn’t help TTFT if launch/dispatch dominates). Both sides agreed to run a small pilot benchmark using Summit-like prompt distributions and Redwood’s harness, then decide kernel-mode defaults + routing guardrails (including fallbacks) before any broader rollout.
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-02-21
Start time: 09:03 AM PT
Duration: 56 min
Title: Quantization performance deep dive (FP8 vs INT8) - Summit AI

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Henry Cho, Hiro Tanaka, Grace Kim, Omar El-Sayed
Summit AI: Ava Chen (CTO), Miguel Santos (Staff ML Eng), Priya Nair (Platform)

Auto-generated notes (Fireflies)
Summary: Discussed FP8/INT8 performance expectations on H100, where wins show up (prefill vs decode), impact of scheduler settings, and quality guardrails. Agreed to run a pilot benchmark with Summit’s distributions and review results.
Action items: (see above)

Transcript
[00:00] Henry Cho: Alright, we’re recording. Cool. Thanks everyone for joining. This is the quantization performance deep dive you asked for. Goal today is basically: your workloads, what you care about, and then where FP8 versus INT8 actually helps in practice, not just like, marketing numbers.

[00:18] Ava Chen: Perfect. Yeah, we’ve been burned by “up to X percent faster” before.

[00:22] Henry Cho: Yep. Understood. Maybe quick round of intros—Ava, Miguel, Priya, and then I’ll pull in Hiro and Grace for the kernel specifics.

[00:31] Miguel Santos: I’m Miguel, I own our inference stack. We do a mix of chat and retrieval, long prompts. We run mostly A100 today, looking at H100 reserved, possibly dedicated.

[00:41] Priya Nair: Priya, platform side. I care about operational stuff, like canarying and not blowing up p95 for paying customers.

[00:48] Henry Cho: Great. Hiro is our serving runtime kernel lead, Grace has been running the FP8/INT8 benchmarks, and Omar is on scheduling.

[00:56] Hiro Tanaka: Hey everyone.

[00:58] Grace Kim: Hi.

[01:00] Omar El-Sayed: Morning.

[01:03] Henry Cho: Ava, want to start with what you’re trying to optimize? Like top 2 metrics.

[01:10] Ava Chen: Sure. We have a paid tier where latency is basically the product. We need p95 time-to-first-token under, call it, 450 milliseconds on our short chat flows. And then on long-context RAG, we care about tail not exploding. Also cost per 1k tokens is getting… gross. Our unit economics are tight.

[01:31] Henry Cho: Got it. When you say long-context, what’s “long” in tokens, roughly?

[01:35] Miguel Santos: Today, typical is 6k to 12k prompt tokens. Worst case we see 20k-ish. Output is usually short, like 150 to 400 tokens, unless summarization, then 1k.

[01:47] Grace Kim: That’s helpful—so you have both prefill-heavy and decode-moderate scenarios.

[01:53] Miguel Santos: Yep. And concurrency: we burst. Like, at peak, 200 concurrent requests across a pool. But per-GPU concurrency we cap by memory, obviously.

[02:03] Henry Cho: And models? Are you pinned to a family? Like Llama 70B class, or smaller?

[02:09] Ava Chen: We use a 70B-ish for highest tier and a smaller one for free tier. We’re not married to a specific open model name, but quality has to hold. We’ve tried quantization before and got weirdness on long prompts.

[02:23] Henry Cho: Yeah, makes sense. Hiro, maybe frame how we think about FP8 vs INT8 and where it can hurt.

[02:30] Hiro Tanaka: Sure. So, the “headline” is: FP8 is generally most friendly on H100 because the hardware path is very mature—Tensor Cores, plus the kernel ecosystem is… more forgiving. INT8 can be faster in certain matmuls but it gets tricky: shape alignment, per-channel scales, calibration. Also attention kernels for INT8 are less uniform across shapes.

[02:54] Miguel Santos: So if we’re H100, FP8 is usually the default “fast path”?

[02:59] Hiro Tanaka: Often, yes, but with caveats. The real answer depends on whether your bottleneck is prefill matmul/attention compute, or if you’re dominated by scheduling overhead, launch overhead, or small-batch decode.

[03:14] Omar El-Sayed: And also whether you’re mixing prefill and decode on the same worker. If you interleave heavily, you can get TTFT regressions even if decode throughput improves.

[03:25] Priya Nair: That’s the part that scares me. We can’t trade TTFT for overall tokens/sec in the wrong direction.

[03:31] Henry Cho: Totally. Let’s break it down by your workloads. Miguel, can you quantify your “short chat” distribution? Prompt length and typical output.

[03:41] Miguel Santos: Short chat is like 200 to 800 input tokens, output 100 to 250 tokens. Lots of system prompt overhead, but not huge.

[03:51] Grace Kim: That’s more decode-balanced. In that regime, you sometimes see quantization wins mostly on decode tokens/sec, but TTFT may not move much. Sometimes it gets slightly worse if the kernel dispatch path adds overhead.

[04:07] Miguel Santos: Slightly worse like… how much?

[04:10] Grace Kim: If things are tuned right, it should be flat-ish within noise. If not tuned—like batching window too aggressive, or a kernel path has higher launch overhead—you can see p95 TTFT regress by, like, tens of milliseconds. Occasionally worse, which is why we do canaries.

[04:29] Ava Chen: We can tolerate +20ms p95 if cost drops. We cannot tolerate +150ms.

[04:35] Henry Cho: Understood. Our process is to gate it per model, per region, and roll with automatic rollback if TTFT crosses a threshold.

[04:44] Priya Nair: Is that something you can do on Dedicated too? Like per-customer cohort.

[04:48] Henry Cho: Yes—Dedicated is actually easier because the pool is isolated. We can enable per-deployment flags.

[04:55] Miguel Santos: What about INT8? We’ve heard it’s “cheaper” somehow.

[04:59] Hiro Tanaka: INT8 can reduce memory bandwidth and sometimes lets you pack more, but the quality and shape constraints can force fallbacks. So the performance story becomes: you might think you’re INT8 but half your traffic is silently running baseline kernels.

[05:16] Grace Kim: And for long-context, the prompt prefill is big. FP8 prefill tends to show clear wins there because you’re doing a lot of GEMM/attention work. INT8 can also win but you need calibration and guardrails; otherwise quality can drift.

[05:33] Ava Chen: When you say quality drift, do you mean like exact match issues or…?

[05:38] Grace Kim: More like: subtle changes. Longer contexts can make it more noticeable: wrong citations, more hallucination, less stable tool calling. Not always, but that’s the failure mode.

[05:50] Miguel Santos: We saw that: tool calling got flaky at long prompt lengths under a quantized model.

[05:55] Omar El-Sayed: Also, when you’re at 12k prompt tokens, your TTFT is mostly prefill. So you’re trading large prefill compute for something faster. That’s where you can win big without changing decode behavior.

[06:07] Henry Cho: Let’s talk H100 specifically. Are you considering H100 SXM, or PCIe? Cloud?

[06:13] Priya Nair: Likely cloud H100, PCIe. We have commitments we can use in us-east and eu-west.

[06:20] Henry Cho: Great. Our fleet standard for H100 PCIe is what most of our numbers will map to.

[06:26] Miguel Santos: Can you share actual numbers today?

[06:29] Henry Cho: On this call, I can give directional ranges, but for anything you want to take internally or to procurement, we need to anchor it in a benchmark run on your distributions. Also our policy is: we footnote driver/CUDA, clocks, and so on. Grace can share methodology and we can do a pilot.

[06:49] Ava Chen: Fair. Directionally is fine.

[06:52] Hiro Tanaka: Directionally: on H100, FP8 paths often improve prefill throughput and overall tokens/sec in the 15–35% range for the right shapes, sometimes more. INT8 matmul can be competitive, but attention path matters a lot. Also, if you’re at low batch, the win shrinks.

[07:11] Miguel Santos: And TTFT?

[07:14] Omar El-Sayed: TTFT is sensitive to scheduling. If you keep batching window conservative and avoid mixing too aggressively, TTFT should be stable; if you try to squeeze max throughput, TTFT can shift. The pilot should measure p50 and p95 TTFT, not just throughput.

[07:32] Priya Nair: Do you have TTFT and TPOT definitions? We’ve seen vendors define them differently.

[07:36] Henry Cho: Yes. We can send metric definitions, like from request accepted time, first token emitted. TPOT as time per output token excluding first token. Grace, we can share the exact counters we use.

[07:49] Grace Kim: Yep.

[07:51] Ava Chen: I want to make sure we’re not comparing apples to oranges. Like streaming flush intervals can skew TTFT.

[07:58] Hiro Tanaka: Good point. For benchmarks, we fix streaming chunking behavior, and we include warmups.

[08:05] Miguel Santos: What about A100? We still have a bunch.

[08:08] Grace Kim: On A100, FP8 is less straightforward because hardware support is different—BF16/FP16 are strong. INT8 can help, but again depends. Usually H100 is where FP8 is the clearest.

[08:20] Ava Chen: So if we go H100 Dedicated, FP8 seems promising.

[08:24] Henry Cho: That’s what we’re seeing across hosted traffic. But we don’t want to over-generalize.

[08:31] Miguel Santos: What workloads don’t benefit?

[08:34] Grace Kim: Very small prompts, very small batches, and anything dominated by overheads. Also, certain shape regimes—like odd head dims or alignment—may trigger fallbacks. And if your model uses certain attention variants, the kernel set changes.

[08:52] Hiro Tanaka: Another case is if your decode is memory-bound and you’re already saturated, quantization helps, but the realized win depends on KV cache behavior and alignment.

[09:03] Miguel Santos: KV cache alignment—yeah we’ve had weird perf cliffs.

[09:07] Hiro Tanaka: Exactly. We’ve fixed some edge cases recently where FP8 decode could regress for certain alignment. That’s why we do shape guardrails.

[09:18] Priya Nair: If it falls back, is that transparent? Like can I see when FP8 was used vs baseline?

[09:23] Henry Cho: In our console you can slice metrics by “kernel mode” and GPU. For Dedicated we can also expose it via metrics tags. We’ll include that in the pilot.

[09:34] Ava Chen: Okay. Let’s talk about our three workloads and what you’d benchmark.

[09:40] Henry Cho: Great. Miguel, can you list them with approximate traffic share?

[09:44] Miguel Santos: 60% short chat (200–800 prompt). 25% RAG, long prompt 6k–12k. 15% summarization, prompt like 2k–4k, output 800–1200.

[09:59] Grace Kim: Perfect. For a pilot, we’d do three representative distributions with fixed concurrency points, say 1, 4, 8, 16 per GPU depending on memory. Then run baseline (FP16/BF16), FP8, INT8 where supported, on H100. Maybe A100 optional.

[10:19] Miguel Santos: And you’d measure TTFT p50/p95, TPOT, tokens/sec, plus error rates?

[10:24] Grace Kim: Yes, and variance across runs. And we’ll pin driver/CUDA and lock clocks if allowed.

[10:33] Priya Nair: Can you lock clocks in our environment? That might be frowned upon.

[10:37] Omar El-Sayed: Optional. If not, we still can reduce variance by isolating nodes and controlling thermals. But variance is a thing.

[10:46] Ava Chen: If we do the pilot in your Dedicated trial, do we get that control easier?

[10:50] Henry Cho: Usually yes, because we can reserve the exact pool and avoid contention.

[10:56] Miguel Santos: But then it’s not our VPC.

[10:58] Henry Cho: Correct. We can do either: start on our pool for speed, then validate in your VPC for security/realism.

[11:07] Priya Nair: Security-wise, we can’t share real prompts. We can share synthetic prompts with similar lengths, and maybe a small anonymized set.

[11:15] Henry Cho: Totally fine. We mostly need the distribution of lengths and some representative content for quality sanity.

[11:23] Ava Chen: What about tool calling? We do function calling style JSON outputs.

[11:28] Grace Kim: We can include a structured-output variant. One caveat: quality regressions show up more in those tasks. So we’d want an eval pass for FP8/INT8.

[11:41] Miguel Santos: How heavy is the eval process?

[11:44] Henry Cho: For a pilot, we do a sanity suite: golden prompts, basic scoring, and we compare to baseline. If it fails, we gate FP8/INT8 for that route or seq-len.

[11:57] Priya Nair: Can gating be seq-len based?

[12:00] Hiro Tanaka: Yes. You can set rules like “FP8 only for prompts > X tokens” or certain shapes. That’s basically how kernel selection heuristics work.

[12:10] Ava Chen: That’s interesting: so we could keep short chat on baseline if TTFT is sensitive and use FP8 for long-context prefill.

[12:18] Omar El-Sayed: Exactly. That’s a common pattern.

[12:22] Miguel Santos: But doesn’t that complicate operations?

[12:25] Henry Cho: A bit, but we can configure it and you monitor by route. The benefit is you get wins where they matter.

[12:34] Priya Nair: Monitoring is key. We need dashboards by model, by region.

[12:39] Henry Cho: Yep. In our canary process we pick one region first, watch TTFT/TPOT, plus error rates and GPU memory headroom.

[12:49] Ava Chen: Okay. Let’s talk cost. How do we translate tokens/sec to cost reduction?

[12:56] Henry Cho: For Hosted, it’s price per token. For Dedicated, it’s basically: can you do more tokens per GPU-hour at stable latency. FP8 improving throughput can reduce required GPU count or improve headroom.

[13:10] Miguel Santos: Our issue is we scale for tail. So if p95 improves, we can shrink.

[13:15] Grace Kim: Exactly. That’s why we emphasize p95.

[13:20] Ava Chen: I’m also wary of “benchmarks” that are just microbench. We want end-to-end.

[13:26] Hiro Tanaka: We do both. Microbench tells us kernel speed. End-to-end includes scheduler, batching, network, streaming. The pilot should be end-to-end serving with realistic concurrency.

[13:39] Miguel Santos: Great.

[13:41] Henry Cho: Let’s get specific about success criteria. Ava, you said p95 TTFT < 450ms for short chat. What about long-context RAG?

[13:51] Ava Chen: For long-context, TTFT is naturally higher. We want p95 under 2.5 seconds for 12k prompts, if possible. And stable—no 6 second spikes.

[14:03] Omar El-Sayed: Those spikes often come from queueing/backpressure. We can instrument queue depth and prefill/decode split to understand.

[14:12] Priya Nair: We’ve seen that too.

[14:15] Miguel Santos: For TPOT, our target is like under 35ms per token on average output, but more important is consistency.

[14:24] Grace Kim: Makes sense.

[14:27] Henry Cho: One more topic: competitors. You mentioned other vendors. Anything you’re seeing there that we should know?

[14:35] Ava Chen: We trialed Together AI and some self-hosting with vLLM. vLLM is good but we don’t want to own the ops. Vendors show nice throughput numbers, but we saw tail issues and canarying wasn’t as mature.

[14:51] Priya Nair: Also on some platforms, “INT8” was basically a black box.

[14:56] Henry Cho: Yeah. Our approach is “quantization with guardrails”: you can see mode, fallback rates, and we can disable per shape if needed.

[15:06] Miguel Santos: Quick question: does FP8 require calibration like INT8?

[15:10] Grace Kim: Usually less than INT8. INT8 often needs calibration data for scales; FP8 is generally less sensitive, but still can have edge cases.

[15:21] Ava Chen: Okay.

[15:23] (crosstalk)
[15:24] Miguel Santos: Sorry—another question: would you recommend FP8 for everything on H100?

[15:28] Hiro Tanaka: Not “everything” blindly. For prefill-heavy and larger batches, yes it’s often a win. For super latency-sensitive short prompts at batch=1, the win might not show and could regress if not tuned. That’s why we do heuristic selection.

[15:45] Omar El-Sayed: And scheduler tuning matters. If you keep batching window too long, TTFT suffers regardless of kernel.

[15:52] Priya Nair: Can you explain the batching window knob in plain English?

[15:56] Omar El-Sayed: Yeah. It’s basically “how long do we wait to collect more requests before launching a batch.” Larger window increases batch size, better GPU efficiency, but adds queueing latency. For short chat, you want it small. For long prefill, you can tolerate slightly bigger.

[16:18] Miguel Santos: So for our mixed workload, we might need separate queues.

[16:21] Omar El-Sayed: Exactly—either separate routes or priority scheduling.

[16:27] Henry Cho: We can help set that up in Dedicated.

[16:31] Ava Chen: Okay. Let’s align on the pilot. What do you need from us?

[16:36] Grace Kim: Three distributions, plus concurrency envelope, plus any constraints (regions, H100 type). And ideally a small set of prompts for quality sanity—anonymized.

[16:49] Miguel Santos: We can do that. For prompts, we can generate synthetic with same lengths. But quality sanity needs real-ish content.

[16:56] Ava Chen: We can share 50 anonymized prompts if legal signs off.

[17:00] Henry Cho: Great. We’ll also send an NDA link if needed.

[17:04] Priya Nair: Another question: do you capture Nsight traces? We’ve had perf mysteries.

[17:09] Hiro Tanaka: Yes, for selected cases. We can capture Nsight Systems/Compute traces in the pilot for top anomalies. Usually we don’t do it for every run because it’s heavy.

[17:23] Miguel Santos: Good.

[17:25] Henry Cho: Timeline: if we send the runbook early next week, can you deliver distributions by end of week?

[17:32] Ava Chen: Probably. Miguel?

[17:34] Miguel Santos: Yes, by Thursday.

[17:36] Henry Cho: Cool. Then we can run the pilot in our Dedicated trial environment Friday/Monday, and review results mid next week.

[17:46] Ava Chen: Works.

[17:48] Priya Nair: On rollout: if we decide to go with FP8, how do you enable gradually?

[17:53] Henry Cho: We start with a canary cohort: one region, small percentage, watch TTFT/TPOT/error rate. Automatic rollback if p95 TTFT regresses beyond threshold for a sustained window.

[18:07] Priya Nair: Sustained window meaning…?

[18:09] Omar El-Sayed: Like, not one spike. We suppress noise by requiring minimum sample sizes.

[18:15] Priya Nair: Good.

[18:18] Miguel Santos: Do you have a “fallback to baseline” per request if a shape is unsupported?

[18:23] Hiro Tanaka: Yes. Kernel registry checks shape constraints, alignment. If it fails, it falls back to baseline kernel. We also track that rate.

[18:34] Ava Chen: Okay.

[18:36] Henry Cho: Any remaining questions about FP8 vs INT8 specifically?

[18:41] Miguel Santos: I guess: is INT8 worth it at all for us, or should we ignore it and focus on FP8 on H100?

[18:49] Grace Kim: For H100, I’d start with FP8. INT8 might still be interesting for cost-focused SKUs or if you have a particular model path where INT8 matmul is clearly faster. But it’s more likely to require calibration + quality checks.

[19:06] Ava Chen: That matches our intuition.

[19:09] Priya Nair: If we wanted to run on L4 for a cheaper tier later, would INT8 matter?

[19:14] Hiro Tanaka: Potentially. L4 has different characteristics. But let’s not boil the ocean—pilot on H100 first.

[19:23] Henry Cho: Agreed.

[19:25] (conversation continues with more detailed Q&A; minor transcription gaps)

[20:03] Miguel Santos: One thing—our bottleneck sometimes is network and streaming overhead. Does that hide kernel wins?

[20:10] Omar El-Sayed: It can. That’s why we also look at server-side metrics: time in queue, time in prefill, time in decode. If kernel gets faster but queue gets worse, you don’t see it end-to-end.

[20:25] Grace Kim: Also, you should measure tokens/sec at the engine level, not just client-perceived.

[20:31] Ava Chen: Makes sense.

[21:02] Henry Cho: Let’s do a quick recap so we’re aligned.

[21:06] Henry Cho: You care about p95 TTFT for short chat (<450ms) and stability for long-context RAG (p95 TTFT < 2.5s at 12k prompt). You want cost reduction but not at the expense of tail. We’ll propose a pilot benchmark with three distributions, run baseline vs FP8 vs INT8 where supported, on H100 PCIe. We’ll include scheduler instrumentation and mode tagging, and we’ll do a quality sanity pass on a small prompt set.

[21:34] Ava Chen: Yep.

[21:36] Miguel Santos: Correct.

[21:38] Priya Nair: And the canary/rollback story is important for us.

[21:42] Henry Cho: Great. We’ll send: benchmark plan, metrics definitions, and a minimal script/runbook by Tuesday. You send distributions and prompts by Thursday. Then we run, and meet mid-week for results.

[21:56] Ava Chen: Sounds good.

[22:00] Henry Cho: Anything else before we drop?

[22:03] Miguel Santos: No, good.

[22:05] Priya Nair: All set.

[22:07] Henry Cho: Cool. Thanks everyone.

(End of transcript. Note: Fireflies truncation—recording continued with a few minutes of scheduling chatter and calendar invites.)
